ch01.anchor: the informers of the concession police stations
ch01.note: In the source, xunbufang (巡捕房), the police stations of Shanghai's foreign concessions (the International Settlement and the French Concession), and baodating (包打聽, literally "hired listen-arounds"), their paid Chinese informers and plainclothes detectives. The author lists them among the ordinary policing bodies with which secret-service work is often confused.

ch01.anchor: Soviet Russia's GPU
ch01.note: The source writes 格伯武, a transliteration of the Russian abbreviation ГПУ (GPU) — the Soviet State Political Directorate, the secret police and political-intelligence organ of 1922-34 (its successor was the OGPU). The commoner Chinese forms are 格別烏/格伯烏. The comparison is apt and pointed: Gu Shunzhang had himself trained in Soviet tradecraft under GPU auspices before building the Chinese Communists' own secret service.

ch01.anchor: special-duty section
ch01.note: A point lost in translation: the word rendered "special-duty" here is the same 特務 (tewu) that the book elsewhere renders "secret service." In an ordinary army or office, 特務股/團/營/連 were mundane guard, escort, and headquarters units. The author is marking off his politically charged "secret-service work" from this older, workaday military sense of the term.

ch01.anchor: the Three Principles of the People
ch01.note: Sun Yat-sen's San Min Zhuyi (三民主義): nationalism, democracy (the people's rights), and the people's livelihood — the official ideology of the Nationalist Party and state.

ch01.anchor: the National Revolution
ch01.note: The Guomin Geming (國民革命), the Nationalist-led revolution of the 1920s — the Northern Expedition of 1926-28 that reunified much of China under the Nationalists — here treated as an ongoing project that secret-service work serves.

ch01.anchor: the Chinese Nationalist Party
ch01.note: The Kuomintang (KMT, Zhongguo Guomindang, 中國國民黨), Sun Yat-sen's party and the ruling party of the Nanjing National Government from 1927. Rendered "the Chinese Nationalist Party" throughout this edition.

ch01.anchor: the vanguard and the special-operations corps
ch01.note: The source has jixianfeng (急先鋒, the spearhead or vanguard) and biedongdui (別動隊), a period military term for detached irregular or special-action units operating apart from the main force.

ch01.anchor: guarding against trouble before it arises
ch01.note: Fang huan wei ran (防患未然), a set phrase — to take precautions before trouble takes shape — with roots in the Book of Changes and the histories.

ch01.anchor: a solid Western-style house upon a patch of sand
ch01.note: The image is the author's own: a yangfang (洋房), a Western-style house, was in 1930s China a byword for solidity and modern substance; a shaqi (沙磧) is a barren flat of sand and gravel. The vividness is kept here as it stands in the source.

ch01.anchor: its opening theme
ch01.note: The source has kaizong mingyi (開宗明義), an allusion to the opening chapter of the Classic of Filial Piety (whose first section is so titled): to state one's governing thesis at the very outset.

ch01.anchor: as the frost underfoot foretells the hard ice, so such things come on by degrees
ch01.note: An allusion to the Book of Changes, the Kun hexagram (坤卦): "When you tread on frost, the hard ice is coming" (履霜堅冰至). The source adds qi lai ye jian (其來也漸), "it comes on by degrees": small early signs presage a great eventual development.

ch01.anchor: a victory that never misses its mark
ch01.note: The source has bai fa bai zhong (百發百中), "a hundred shots, a hundred hits" — every stroke tells.

ch01.anchor: win a hundred battles out of a hundred
ch01.note: An allusion to Sunzi's Art of War: "Know the enemy and know yourself, and in a hundred battles you will never be in peril" (知彼知己，百戰不殆). The book prints 知已 for 知己 ("know yourself"), a common orthographic slip, and gives the more colloquial 百戰百勝, "win every one of a hundred battles."

ch01.anchor: some five million gold pounds a year
ch01.note: These figures — some five million gold pounds a year for Britain, half of the budget for Japan's military and a third of that for its "secret" fund — are the author's assertions of 1933, offered to impress rather than from any audited account, and are best read as uncorroborated period claims.

ch01.anchor: In our war with Japan
ch01.note: Writing in mid-1933 (the preface is dated July 1933), the author means the undeclared Sino-Japanese fighting of 1931-33 — the Mukden Incident and the loss of Manchuria (September 1931), the Shanghai war of early 1932, and the Rehe and Great Wall campaign of 1933 — not the full-scale war that began in 1937.

ch01.anchor: the Second World War will one day break out in the Pacific
ch01.note: A strikingly prescient forecast for 1933: the Pacific War duly opened with Japan's attacks on Pearl Harbor and Southeast Asia in December 1941. The claim is corroborated by events, though of course the author could not have known their shape.

ch01.anchor: the sili and siji of the Zhou, or the xiangting and youjiao of the Qin and Han
ch01.note: Real historical offices (verified against the scan: 司隸, 司稽, 鄉亭, 游徼). In the Rites of Zhou the sili (司隸) oversaw convict labour and menial guards and the siji (司稽) was a market inspector who patrolled for wrongdoing; xiangting (鄉亭) refers to the township-and-tithing 亭 posts of Qin-Han local government, whose 亭長 kept order and ran the postal relay, and the youjiao (游徼) was a local patrol officer charged with catching bandits. The author's point — that these were only the embryo of ordinary policing, not political intelligence — is fair; 司隸 is in fact better known in its Han form, the powerful sili xiaowei (司隸校尉) who supervised the capital region.

ch01.anchor: split of 1927
ch01.note: The violent rupture of the First United Front: Chiang Kai-shek's purge of the Communists in Shanghai on 12 April 1927 and the subsequent break at Wuhan, after which the Chinese Communist Party went underground and built the clandestine apparatus the author goes on to describe. Corroborated.

ch01.anchor: it began with the C.P.
ch01.note: C.P. is the author's own abbreviation for the Communist Party. The admission carries an irony he does not spell out: Gu Shunzhang was himself the head of the Communists' Central Special Branch — the very apparatus he credits here as "formidable" — until his defection to the Nationalists in April 1931. This manual is his account of the tradecraft he built and then turned against its makers.

ch01.anchor: reach a pitch of consummate mastery
ch01.note: The source has chushen ruhua (出神入化), literally "entering the divine and passing into the transformed": a supreme, almost magical command of one's art.

ch01.anchor: the Ministry of Communications
ch01.note: The Jiaotong Bu (交通部), the real Republican government ministry for posts, telegraph, railways, and shipping. The author is playing on the word 交通: in tradecraft it means clandestine liaison and courier work, not public transport.

ch01.anchor: runs on the banks
ch01.note: The source has jidui (擠兌), a rush to redeem banknotes or withdraw deposits. Engineering a bank run against the enemy is listed here, coolly, among the methods of economic sabotage.

ch01.anchor: local bullies and evil gentry
ch01.note: Tuhao lieshen (土豪劣紳), a stock label of the National Revolution for rural power-holders — landlord bosses and corrupt gentry — marked out as targets. The fixed pairing is kept.

ch01.anchor: iron discipline
ch01.note: The source has 鋼的紀律, literally "steel discipline" — the Leninist ideal of a tightly bound party organisation, a vocabulary the author carries over from the Communist apparatus he had served.

ch01.anchor: one-party rule of the Chinese Nationalist Party
ch01.note: Yidang zhuanzheng (一黨專政), literally "one-party dictatorship" — the doctrine of Nationalist party tutelage formalised under the 1931 provisional constitution.

ch02.anchor: Soviet Russia has its State Political Directorate
ch02.note: The source writes 國家政治檢察局, one of several Chinese renderings of the Soviet ГПУ (GPU). The commoner form is 國家政治保衛局 ("State Political Directorate"); the manual elsewhere transliterates the initials as 格伯武 (see the note on the GPU in ch. 1). The point here is structural: the GPU served as the open, avowed face of a security apparatus whose real work stayed secret, and the author holds it up as the model for a "public organ" fronting a clandestine one — the very arrangement he goes on to prescribe.

ch02.anchor: Diagram of the Central Secret-Service Organization
ch02.note: The appended plate (reproduced here) sets out a chain of command reading, from the top: the Central Political Bureau (中央政治局) → a Central Secret-Service Conference (中央特務會議) → the Central Secret-Service Headquarters, in parenthesis the Central Defense Bureau (中央特務總部（中央保衛局）), with its office (辦公處), flanked by a Secret-Service Work Training Class (特務工作訓練班) and a Secret-Service Statistics Research Society (特務統計研究會). Below sit four departments — First, Observation (觀察); Second, Inquiry (探訪); Third, Protection (保護); Fourth, Communications (交通) — the Inquiry department subdividing into numbered sections (科) and sub-sections (股); a dashed line runs down to the Secret-Service Departments of the provinces and regions (各省區特務部). It is an idealized blueprint, not a record of an apparatus already in being.

ch02.anchor: Diagram of the Distribution of the Detective Network
ch02.note: The plate places the Central Inquiry Department (中央探訪部) at the hub, radiating to eight regional areas — North China, the Northeast, East China, Central China, South China, the Southwest, West China, and the Northwest — each ringed by the abbreviated names of its provinces, which subdivide in turn into counties and cities; at the base the net reaches into Party, government, army, and police organs, and further into ministries, professions, schools, social bodies, and the secret societies (幫會). The scheme is comprehensive by design — a map of total penetration rather than a report of penetration achieved.

ch02.anchor: Diagram of the Distribution of the Communications Network
ch02.note: The plate mirrors the detective-network chart: a Central Communications Station (交通總站) at the hub feeds regional stations (區站), which feed provincial branch stations (分站), which feed local sub-stations (小站) — the same eight-region frame applied to the movement of messages rather than the gathering of them.

ch02.anchor: the gang rules of the Green and Red Gangs
ch02.note: 青紅幫: the two great Shanghai secret-society traditions — the Green Gang (青幫), rooted in the Grand Canal grain-transport guilds and the Luo sect, and the Hong or Red Gang (紅幫 / 洪門), the anti-Qing sworn-brotherhood tradition. The example is pointed: the author, Gu Shunzhang, was himself a Green Gang initiate, and his fluency in its discipline and cellular secrecy was part of what made him so effective a secret-police chief (Green Gang: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Gang).

鋼的紀律, literally "steel discipline." The metaphor and the demand behind it are Leninist party-discipline carried into tradecraft — iron obedience, vertical command, no horizontal ties — and the author, who built the Chinese Communists' security apparatus before turning it against them, reproduces the idiom even while writing for the Nationalist side.

ch02.anchor: serves Qin in the morning and Chu by evening
ch02.note: 朝秦暮楚: a Warring States image for fickle allegiance — a small state (or a man) caught between the rival powers of Qin and Chu, siding now with one and now with the other. Here, shifting political loyalty.

ch02.anchor: a hundred temperings make steel and a thousand make gold
ch02.note: 百鍊成鋼，千鍊成金: a proverbial pairing — metal is made sound only by being worked over and over in the fire — for the making of a person through repeated hard trial. The author applies it to the seasoning of an agent.

ch02.anchor: better a vacancy than a poor fit
ch02.note: 寧缺毋濫: literally "rather leave it short than let it overflow" — better a post left empty than one filled carelessly with the unfit. A standard maxim of selective recruitment.

ch02.anchor: a general is easy to recruit and hard to dismiss
ch02.note: 招將容易退將難: a proverb — it is easy to take a general on, hard to send him away again. The application: because an agent, once admitted, carries the organization's secrets, taking on the wrong person is far costlier here than in ordinary work.

ch02.anchor: no one is born with knowledge
ch02.note: 人非生而知之，乃係學而知之: an echo of the Analects, where Confucius ranks "those born knowing" above "those who know through learning" (Ji shi) and elsewhere disclaims the first rank for himself — wo fei sheng er zhi zhi zhe (Shu er). The author turns it to a practical end: agents are made, not found, and must be taught without cease.

ch02.anchor: putting his subjects to death without having taught them
ch02.note: 不教而誅: from the Analects (Yao yue), where 不教而殺 — to execute people without having first instructed them — is named the first of the "four evils" of misgovernment. The author invokes it to condemn discipline imposed without published, knowable rules: punishment at one man's whim rather than by law.

ch02.anchor: punish one and so warn a hundred
ch02.note: 懲一儆百: to punish one person as a warning to a hundred — to make an example. A standard idiom of deterrence.

ch02.anchor: the schools run by the Shanghai Municipal Council
ch02.note: 上海工部局: the Shanghai Municipal Council, the (foreign-run) governing body of the International Settlement, whose police force — the Shanghai Municipal Police, the Settlement's 捕房 — maintained welfare provision and schooling for its personnel. The author, who operated for years in Settlement Shanghai, takes it as a model for how a service should provide for its people's children (Shanghai Municipal Police: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Municipal_Police).

ch02.anchor: He is like a first-rate bomb
ch02.note: The manual's most vivid figure for the agent as capital asset: a bomb of the best make is thrown only in extremity and must then fetch ten times its cost, and is otherwise stored with care against needless loss. The passage says plainly that safeguarding an agent's life is not humanity but husbandry — "the husbanding of the organization's own strength."

ch02.anchor: spit in his face and wait for it to dry of itself
ch02.note: 唾面自乾: a Tang-dynasty phrase. The statesman Lou Shide counselled his brother that if a man spat in his face he should not even wipe it away but let it dry of itself — the very model of forbearance. The author inverts the classical praise: here such a man is no paragon of patience but a dull, spineless sort, unfit for the work.

自我批評 ("self-criticism"), together with the 批評會 ("criticism meeting") in the same list and the preference just above for the 啟發式 (heuristic) method over the 灌輸式 (rote "pouring-in") method: these are the training and rectification techniques of the Communist organization in which the author was formed, set down here in a handbook written for its enemies.

ch02.anchor: The organization should be divided into three layers
ch02.note: An inset diagram (reproduced here) accompanies this principle: three concentric circles — the innermost the core (中心), the middle ring the cadre elements (幹部份子), the outer ring the bought-over and utilized elements (收買及利用份子). The scheme returns in §6, where the author notes that the outer ring is recruited precisely by playing on ordinary people's love of gain.

報務員 and 譯電員: the radio operator who works the key, and the clerk who encodes and decodes the traffic. That the manual already treats wireless telegraphy and ciphered communications as core tradecraft reflects the technical level of the Communist underground the author had run, whose clandestine radio links were among its signal achievements.

ch03.anchor: Still as a virgin, then breaking out like a bolting hare
ch03.note: The book cites this as a saying from “the art of war” (兵法), and it does descend from Sunzi’s Art of War (孫子·九地, “The Nine Terrains”), whose text runs shi ru chu nü, diren kai hu; hou ru tuo tu, di bu ji ju — “at first be like a virgin, and the enemy opens his door; then be like a bolting hare, and the enemy cannot resist.” It is usually quoted in the polished four-character form 静如處女，動如脱兔 (“still as a virgin, moving like a bolting hare”); Gu’s 出如脱兔 (“breaking out like a bolting hare”) is a common variant. Corroborated against the received text.

ch03.anchor: where neither god nor ghost perceives it
ch03.note: 神不知鬼不覺, literally “gods do not know it, ghosts do not sense it” — a set idiom for something done in perfect, undetectable secrecy. Kept literal for its flavor.

ch03.anchor: grasping one thing and missing ten thousand
ch03.note: 掛一漏萬, literally “hang up one, let ten thousand slip”: to attend to a single item and overlook countless others. The image survives whole in the English.

ch03.anchor: like quicksilver spilt on the ground, entering at every pore
ch03.note: 如水銀瀉地，無孔不入 — “like quicksilver poured out on the ground, entering wherever there is a crack.” A vivid idiom for total, seeping penetration; the manual applies it to the reach it wants for its intelligence coverage.

點石成金 (“touch a stone and make it gold”), an image from Daoist alchemical lore of the immortals’ transmuting touch, long since a byword for a magical, too-good-to-be-true feat. Gu uses it against itself: the conjurer’s gold is a trick, whereas secret-service work must rest on fact.

紙上談兵, “to discuss soldiering on paper” — empty theorizing divorced from practice. The phrase is conventionally attached to Zhao Kuo (趙括), the Zhao commander whose bookish generalship brought catastrophe at Changping in 260 BC (told in the Records of the Grand Historian); note, though, that the four-character idiom itself is a much later coinage, since paper did not yet exist in the Warring States. The attribution to Zhao Kuo is the standard one, with that caveat.

匪區, the Nationalist term for territory held by the Communists — the “bandit” (匪) label the government of the day fastened on the CCP and its rural base areas, the same usage that named the “bandit-suppression” (剁匪) military campaigns of the early 1930s. Rendered literally to keep the period standpoint the manual is written from; the author, a Communist security chief turned Nationalist, adopts his new employers’ vocabulary.

社會化 (shèhuìhuà), literally “socialization,” but in this manual a term of tradecraft: the agent’s dissolving of himself into the ordinary life around him so as to pass unnoticed. Gu treats it as a whole discipline and defers its detailed treatment to a later section — it becomes the subject of Chapter 7, “Blending Into Society.”

ch03.anchor: carrying on his work in secret
ch03.note: The character rendered “in secret” here (暗中進行, “carry on covertly”) sits directly beneath the round National Central Library seal stamped across this page, and the 進 of 進行 is largely obscured by it. The reading 暗中進行 is the natural collocation and is adopted with that qualification; nothing turns on it for the sense.

ch04.note: 中心思想, literally “central thought” — the governing idea or core conviction from which a person’s judgments and conduct proceed. Rendered “central conviction” here for the settling, orienting sense the passage gives it: the thing that keeps the will from being shaken. (The same two words can elsewhere mean merely the “main idea” of a text.)

ch04.anchor: wind and frost and rain and dew
ch04.note: 風霜雨露, “wind, frost, rain and dew” — a set image for the accumulated trials and buffetings of circumstance. Kept literal for its weathering force.

觀念鬥爭, the section title, literally “the struggle over ideas / over mindset.” The Chinese-language table of contents rendered it “Building the Right Mindset,” which is an interpretation; the text describes not a building-up but a contest — two opposing 觀念 warring in the mind until one wins. The phrase also carries the flavor of the Marxist 思想鬥爭 (“ideological struggle”) vocabulary that the author, a former Communist intelligence chief, knew intimately, here turned to a Nationalist and individual-conscience purpose. Translated faithfully as “the struggle over mindset.”

十萬元 — one hundred thousand yuan. In 1933 this meant silver yuan (the paper fabi currency was not introduced until 1935), an immense sum. The temptation the author then sketches — a foreign-style house, a motor-car, Western dining — is the lifestyle of the treaty-port rich; the figure is deliberately extravagant, to make the moral test as stark as possible.

吃大菜, literally “eat the big dishes.” 大菜 (dàcài) was the standard Republican-era Shanghai word for Western food or a Western-style restaurant meal, alongside 西餐 and 番菜; Fuzhou Road’s Western restaurants were known as the 四馬路大菜. To dine on 大菜 was a marker of Westernized wealth, which is why it stands here beside the foreign house and the motor-car. Corroborated: Shanghai used 大菜 for Western cuisine from the 1870s.

其間豈可以道里相計呢, “how could the distance between them be reckoned in li?” The 里 (li) is the Chinese mile, in this period roughly half a kilometer. 道里相計, “to measure by the road-distance in li,” is an idiom for gauging how far apart two things stand; paired with 有如天高地下 (“as far as heaven is above the earth”) it insists the gulf between his old poverty and the offered wealth is past all measuring. Kept literal.

ch04.anchor: sinks to a Jie or a Zhou
ch04.note: From the couplet 天機一轉，得為聖賢，一念之差，降為桀紂 — “let the workings of Heaven turn once and one may rise to a sage; let a single thought go astray and one sinks to a Jie or a Zhou.” 桀 (Jie) was the last king of the Xia and 紂 (Zhou, i.e. King Zhou of Shang / 帝辛) the last of the Shang; in the Confucian moral tradition they are the paradigm tyrants, the standing antithesis of the sage-kings Yao and Shun. The whole moral distance between sage and monster can turn on one thought — which is exactly the weight the author assigns to the struggle over mindset.

ch04.anchor: climbing a tree to look for fish
ch04.note: 緣木求魚, “to climb a tree in search of fish” — a byword for a method doomed to fail, from Mencius (孟子·梁惠王上), where Mencius tells King Xuan of Qi that to seek hegemony by force of arms is like climbing a tree for fish. Gu sharpens it: in Mencius the folly is at least harmless (“though you get no fish, no calamity follows”), whereas the false-minded agent, Gu warns, will not merely get no result but court a far greater danger — which is in fact Mencius’s fuller point, that pursuing the wrong end wholeheartedly brings disaster after. Corroborated against the Mencius text.

ch04.anchor: treat their comrades as hired hands
ch04.note: The source reads 勿以官僚化自居，而以僱傭化對待同志 — literally “do not set yourself up in a bureaucratic manner, and treat comrades in a hireling manner.” The second clause carries no second 勿 (“do not”), so on its face it reads as an instruction to treat comrades as hirelings, which is plainly the reverse of the sense; the negative of the first clause has to be understood as governing the second, and it is so rendered here. 僱傭化 (“hireling-ization,” the mercenary spirit) is the same vice condemned at length in Chapter 3, §2.

ch05.note: The idiom is shou kou ru ping (守口如瓶), literally "guard the mouth as one guards a bottle" — keep it stoppered so nothing spills. It is old and proverbial and is the standard Chinese phrase for absolute discretion.

ch05.anchor: no wind gets through, and no rain leaks in
ch05.note: A common saying, feng bu tou, yu bu lou (風不透,雨不漏): watertight and airtight, nothing gets in or out. Gu uses it for the second face of secrecy — not a single thing about the organization allowed to escape.

ch05.anchor: deep moats and high ramparts, drawn up in full array to await us
ch05.note: Two military set-phrases run together: shen gou gao lei (深溝高壘), "deep moats and high ramparts," the classic image of an entrenched, prepared defense; and yan zhen yi dai (嚴陣以待), "to wait in strict battle order." The point is that a forewarned enemy digs in and lies in wait.

Baotan (包探): a plainclothes detective or paid informer of the Shanghai police, especially the foreign-concession forces. The word carried a distinctly sinister ring in the underground world of the period; such men, and the landlords or hoodlums tied to them, were the first hazard in choosing a safe house.

Shenzhuang zihao (申莊字號): Shen (申) is a literary name for Shanghai, and a shenzhuang was a firm's Shanghai purchasing-and-shipping branch; zihao is a trade name. As a cover it explained a steady stream of callers and parcels.

Niangyi (娘姨) is the Shanghai (Wu-dialect) word for a live-in female domestic servant. Gu lists her among the household roles — parents, wife, children, siblings, maid — that a "family" cover apparatus must cast and rehearse until no one can tell it is a sham.

A tongxianghui (同鄉會), an association of people from the same home district — ubiquitous in migrant Shanghai. Because such bodies handled real correspondence and lodging for their members, they made a natural, unremarkable shell for a communications apparatus.

Xunbu (巡捕): a uniformed constable of a foreign concession's police — the Shanghai Municipal Police of the International Settlement or the French Concession force. (The station, the xunbufang/捕房, was glossed earlier in the book.) They are named here beside the ordinary Chinese police as the neighborhood eyes an agent must never let recognize him at an apparatus door.

Two fixtures of the Shanghai lilong (lane-house) world: the jingzu zhangfang (經租賬房), the agent who collected rents and kept the books for a sublandlord, and the kan-nong ren (看弄人), the man who watched the mouth of the lane. Both saw everyone who came and went, so an apparatus's occupants had to keep a single consistent story with them.

ch05.anchor: The Communist Party's central organs have of late been broken up again and again
ch05.note: Written by a defector in 1933, this is Gu's own account of the disaster he himself set off. The documented catastrophe was Gu Shunzhang's capture at Wuhan on 24 April 1931 and immediate defection, after which he betrayed the Central Special Branch's Shanghai networks — safe houses, communication hubs, and cadres — leading to mass arrests and the branch's effective dissolution. Here he generalizes the lesson: the courier is the thread by which a whole network is unravelled. See the fuller note at the 1930 case below.

ch05.anchor: in 1930 a Party communications man on the Shanghai side
ch05.note: Minguo shijiu nian (民國十九年) is the nineteenth year of the Republic, i.e. 1930. Gu dates the awakening to a 1930 courier who was spotted, collapsing the important organs across Shanghai's "seven great districts." No single 1930 incident of this scale is corroborated in the standard literature; the well-documented general collapse of the CCP's Shanghai underground came the following year, in April 1931, and was triggered by Gu's own defection (see Wikipedia, "Gu Shunzhang," and CIA Studies in Intelligence 56:3, 2012). The 1930 dating should be read as the author's own, possibly self-serving, framing rather than an established date.

Chao bazi (抄把子), more usually written chao bazi 抄靶子 — Shanghai slang for a police stop-and-search, and by extension the constables (often Sikh or Chinese) who carried it out, frisking passers-by at will. The threat of a sudden body search, gun drawn, is the recurring nightmare of this chapter's courier.

ch05.anchor: write with an infusion of gallnut, develop with green vitriol
ch05.note: This is iron-gall chemistry: wubeizi (五倍子), the Chinese gallnut, is rich in tannic and gallic acid, and lüfan (綠礬), "green vitriol," is ferrous sulfate; brushed over the dried tannin writing, the iron reacts to form black iron-gall ink and the message appears. The same reaction underlies traditional iron-gall writing ink.

The scan prints lühua gu (綠化鈷), an apparent misprint for lühua gu 氯化鈷, cobalt(II) chloride. Cobalt chloride is the classic heat-developed invisible ink: written faint and near-invisible when damp, it turns blue as gentle heat drives off the water of hydration, and fades again as it reabsorbs moisture — exactly the "heated it comes out blue" the text describes.

ch05.anchor: ultraviolet light, say, or infrared, or cathode rays
ch05.note: Gu's terms are ziwai guang (紫外光, ultraviolet), wai-hong guang (外紅光, i.e. 紅外, infrared), and yinji fangshexian (陰極放射線, cathode rays). Inks that fluoresce or absorb only under UV or IR, read off with a special lamp and leaving the paper unmarked, were a genuine and then-advanced branch of secret writing; the description is technically sound for 1933.

ch05.anchor: one man hides a thing, and eighteen cannot find it
ch05.note: A proverb, yi ren cang wu, shiba ren nan xun (一人藏物,十八人難尋): what one person conceals, a dozen and more cannot dig out. Gu couples it with his maxim that the work is dou zhi not dou li — a contest of wits, not of strength.

Yuejing dai (月經帶), the cloth menstrual/sanitary belt worn before disposable products. Gu lists it, with the hair-bun, as a hiding place available to a woman courier — a candid instance of tradecraft exploiting a search's social taboos.

Loug e fa (漏格法), the grille cipher (the Cardan grille): a mask with holes cut at pre-agreed positions is laid over a sheet, the secret words written through the holes, and an innocuous letter composed around them; the recipient reads the message by laying an identical grille over it. Gu's insistence that the cover-text "read smoothly and in good sense" is the method's real difficulty.

The reference is to the Chinese commercial telegraph code (mingma 明碼), the standard book that assigned each character a four-digit group for wiring. Gu's three tricks — taking the neighboring group left/right or above/below in the code table, or adding/subtracting a fixed figure — are simple superencipherments laid on top of that public code, so that an interceptor reading the plain code book still cannot recover the text.

ch05.anchor: the Sincere Company, the Wing On Company
ch05.note: Xianshi (先施, the Sincere Co., opened on Nanjing Road in 1917) and Yong'an (永安, Wing On, opened 1918 directly across the street) were two of the "four great" modern department stores of pre-war Shanghai. Their printed wrapping paper, branded cord, and uniformed delivery men were exactly the everyday commercial camouflage Gu recommends for moving a parcel of documents. (Corroborated; see standard histories of Nanjing Road commerce.)

ch05.anchor: set up a wireless-manufacturing works of one's own
ch05.note: In this sentence the scan prints dianwu yuan as 店務員 (shop clerk), an evident misprint for 電務員, the radio operator — the same radio-operators' training class named correctly a few pages earlier. It is rendered here as "radio-operators" to match.

ch05.anchor: fire off the big guns about it
ch05.note: Fang da pao (放大砲), literally "to fire the big cannon" — to talk big, to boast loudly of what one has not yet done. The image is kept for its bluster.

ch05.anchor: must not let his edge show
ch05.note: Lu feng mang (露鋒鋩): to let the point and edge of the blade show — to display one's sharpness or acuity. The agent in conversation should keep his cleverness sheathed.

ch06.anchor: may be studied under the following heads
ch06.note: The source enumerates four heads of disguise but misnumbers them: it prints 一 (I) for Dress, 二 (II) for the Face, then 四 (IV) twice — once for Speech and once for Identity — skipping 三 (III) altogether. The four-part structure is plainly intended, so this translation renumbers them I–IV in order; the doubling is a printer's slip, not a feature of the text.

ch06.anchor: his real face of Mount Lu
ch06.note: Lushan zhen mianmu (廬山真面目), "the true face of Mount Lu": a set phrase from Su Shi's (蘇軾, 1037–1101) poem Written on the Wall of West Forest Temple — "I cannot know the true face of Mount Lu, / only because I am myself within the mountain." It means a thing's real nature, hidden from the viewer. Here, the agent's own true identity.

ch06.anchor: you get a dog instead
ch06.note: Two idioms in one sentence. "Do not wait until you are thirsty to dig the well" is lin ke jue jing (臨渴掘井): to prepare only when the need is already upon you. "Setting out to draw a tiger, you get a dog instead" is hua hu bu cheng fan lei quan (畫虎不成反類犬): to attempt something beyond one's skill and produce a botched, ridiculous result.

ch06.anchor: felt "basin" hat
ch06.note: The tongpen mao (銅盆帽), literally "copper-basin hat": a hard round-crowned felt hat resembling an inverted basin (of the bowler/derby family). The guapi xiaomao (瓜皮小帽), "melon-rind skullcap," is the traditional segmented Chinese skullcap. Swapping the stiff Western-style hat for the soft native cap changes the wearer's apparent class and dress at a stroke.

ch06.anchor: the picking-up of a girl on the street
ch06.note: Diao bangzi (吊膀子), Shanghai (Wu) slang for flirtatious street pickup — literally "dangling arms," from a man contriving to link arms with a woman. The manual takes it as the everyday analogue of tailing: both demand patience, nerve, and reading the other person, and both fail if done clumsily.

ch06.anchor: losing the lady and the soldiers both
ch06.note: Pei le furen you zhe bing (賠了夫人又折兵): from the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, where Zhou Yu's scheme to trap Liu Bei by marrying him to Sun Quan's sister backfires — Liu Bei carries off the bride and Zhou Yu's troops are beaten too. Proverbial for a stratagem that recoils into a double loss.

ch06.anchor: one unit of capital and ten-thousandfold profit
ch06.note: Yi ben wan li (一本萬利): "a single unit of capital, ten-thousandfold return" — a tiny outlay yielding an enormous gain. The one man shadowed, if he leads to the whole apparatus, is such a return.

ch06.anchor: let no horse's hoof show
ch06.note: Lu chu ma jiao (露出馬腳), "to let the horse's leg show": to betray oneself, give the game away — as a pantomime horse is exposed when a real leg pokes out from under the costume. Kept literal here because the manual's whole subject is the telltale sign.

ch06.anchor: an old hand at shadowing work
ch06.note: Lao menkan (老門檻), Shanghai (Wu) slang for a wily veteran, an old stager who knows every trick — literally "old threshold," one who has crossed the same doorsill so often he knows it blind.

ch06.anchor: white characters on a black ground
ch06.note: Corroborated. Motor plates in the Shanghai International Settlement were indeed black with white characters (the Settlement issued China's first automobile plates, from 1902), while the Chinese-administered municipality used the Nationalist blue-and-white scheme of the "blue sky, white sun." A car crossing between jurisdictions might carry several plates at once. The book's detail is accurate to 1930s Shanghai.

ch06.anchor: the third-class car
ch06.note: Shanghai's trams ran classed carriages at different fares; a passenger's class signalled his social station, so the shadower rides the class his disguise fits — third class in ordinary clothes, first class (頭等) in a Western suit — to sit near the quarry without seeming out of place.

ch06.anchor: coming by way of Vladivostok
ch06.note: Haishenwai (海參崴), the Chinese name for Vladivostok, the Russian Pacific port and a common transit point for Chinese students returning from the USSR. The "international detective" (國際偵探) of the anecdote is a foreign-concession or treaty-port investigator; the tale is the author's illustrative parable, not a documented case, and is offered as one.

ch06.anchor: counter-counter-surveillance
ch06.note: The passage turns on a chain of 偵探 (zhentan, "detective / to detect"): 反偵探 (fan zhentan, counter-surveillance) is placing the enemy's detectives under surveillance, and 反反偵探 ("counter-counter-surveillance") is surveilling their surveillance of ours. The recursion is deliberate in the source; "counter-surveillance" is kept throughout for consistency with the term as it is used elsewhere in the book.

ch06.anchor: escaping the tiger's mouth
ch06.note: A cluster of idioms of hopeless peril: shen ru hu kou (深入虎口), deep into the tiger's mouth; wan wu sheng lu (萬無生路), not one road to life in ten thousand; bi deng tian hai nan (比登天還難), harder than climbing to heaven. Kept literal, as the register is deliberately vivid.

ch06.anchor: the lines of our own palm
ch06.note: Liao ru zhi zhang (瞭如指掌), "as clear as looking at the lines of one's own palm": to know a thing perfectly, in complete detail.

ch06.anchor: the Communist Party above all
ch06.note: The parenthesis is the author's: 「尤其是共產黨」, "especially the Communist Party." Gu Shunzhang (顧順章) had been the Chinese Communist Party's own chief of security and intelligence until his capture and defection to the Nationalists in 1931; this handbook turns the tradecraft he built for the CCP against it. The counsel to plant agents inside the enemy's detective apparatus is written by a man who had run exactly that apparatus.

ch06.anchor: the attitude of affection and sincerity
ch06.note: Qin'ai jingcheng (親愛精誠), "affection and sincerity" — the motto proclaimed by Sun Yat-sen at the founding of the Whampoa Military Academy in 1924 and, by the 1930s, a stock Nationalist watchword for comradely solidarity. The author invokes it for the warmth comrades owe one another as men, even as he insists they watch one another in the work.

ch06.anchor: no lateral tie in the work
ch06.note: Heng de guanxi (橫的關係), "horizontal / lateral relations": the compartmentalization rule set out in the chapter on organization — comrades are linked only vertically, up to a controller, never sideways to one another, so that no one taken can betray more than his own thread.

ch06.anchor: using your own spear to attack your own shield
ch06.note: Yi zi zhi mao, gong zi zhi dun (以子之矛，攻子之盾): from the Han Feizi parable of the hawker who boasted that his spear would pierce any shield and his shield stop any spear — the source of the modern word for "contradiction" (矛盾). Here it means turning the enemy's own device back upon him.

ch06.anchor: carries home a great wooden dummy for his pains
ch06.note: The source has the enemy's agent 扛囘一個大木梢 / 扛一個木梢囘去 — literally "shoulder home a wooden shao." It is a slangy play on shao (梢, the "tail" of 釘梢, shadowing): instead of a live lead the dupe is sent off lugging a dead wooden stick — a decoy, a worthless result. The reading of this local expression is provisional; "wooden dummy" renders the sense.

ch06.anchor: the stratagem of sowing discord
ch06.note: Fan jian ji (反間計), the counter-espionage or double-agent stratagem — the thirty-third of the traditional Thirty-Six Stratagems (三十六計): turning the enemy's own spies, or planting false intelligence through them, to set the enemy against himself.

ch06.anchor: throw himself into the net
ch06.note: Zi tou luo wang (自投羅網), "to hurl oneself into the net": to walk unwittingly into a trap of one's own accord.

ch06.anchor: the spring silkworm bound fast in its own thread
ch06.note: Two idioms. Nong qiao cheng zhuo (弄巧成拙): to overreach in cleverness and bungle the thing. The image that follows is chun can zi fu (春蠶自縛), "the spring silkworm binds itself" — the book's variant of the commoner zuo jian zi fu (作繭自縛), spinning the cocoon that traps you. The scan reads 春蠶, printed clearly, so the variant is the author's, not a misreading.

ch06.anchor: sent by the Shanghai Garrison Command
ch06.note: The Shanghai Garrison Command (上海衞戍司令部) was the Nationalist military garrison headquarters for the Shanghai area under the Nanjing government; through the late 1920s and 1930s it was an instrument of the anti-Communist suppression in which the author himself had been a central figure before his 1931 defection.

ch06.anchor: carrying a Mauser pistol
ch06.note: The source has 駁殼鎗 (bokeqiang), the Chinese name for the Mauser C96 — the “broomhandle” semi-automatic pistol with its distinctive wooden holster-stock, also called 盒子炮 (“box cannon”) or 匣子槍. Imported and copied in enormous numbers, it was the signature sidearm of Republican-era soldiers, bodyguards, and assassins.

ch06.anchor: that sold by the Kwong Sang firm is best
ch06.note: 廣生行, romanized here as Kwong Sang Hong in its own Cantonese form, was a well-known Hong Kong–Shanghai toiletries house founded in 1898, famous above all for its “Two Girls” (雙妹) Florida Water and cosmetics. Its appearance here as a purveyor of gun-cleaning oil is uncorroborated and sits oddly with its cosmetics trade; the book may mean a broader general-goods line sold under the same well-recognized name, or a like-named shop. The rendering of the name is provisional.

ch06.anchor: a bore of about 7.65
ch06.note: The bores named — 7.65 and 6.35 (millimetres) — are the two standard pocket-pistol calibres of the period: 7.65 mm is the .32 ACP (7.65×17 Browning) and 6.35 mm the .25 ACP (6.35×16 Browning). The “six-inch” and “four-inch” classes (六寸/四寸, measured in the Chinese cun) are rough overall-length categories used in the era's arms trade rather than exact figures; the calibre-to-size correspondence the book gives is broadly consistent with the market it describes.

ch06.anchor: (1) Germany is best
ch06.note: The ranking reflects the interwar reputation of the European pistol trade: German makes (Mauser, and the Luger and Walther houses) were the benchmark, while Spain — the Astra, Star and countless “Ruby”-type workshops of Eibar — was the great source of cheaper copies flooding into China. The judgement is the author's own and reflects perceived quality, not a formal standard.

ch06.anchor: The gas-gun is a recent invention
ch06.note: 毒氣鎗 (“gas-gun”) here is a concealable pistol firing a lachrymatory (tear-gas) round, not a lethal firearm — consistent with the text's own statement that the small type “absolutely cannot” kill and that a victim revives within minutes. The book's claim of Japanese origin is uncorroborated. The original's detailed account of the cartridge's internal composition has been omitted from this edition (see the editorial note below).

ch06.anchor: the malacca baton
ch06.note: The source reads 麻力樹棍. 麻力 is most likely a transliteration of malacca (the malacca or rattan cane long used for police truncheons), giving “malacca stick”; the reading is provisional, as 麻力 could instead be a brand or trade name. The reference is to the batons carried by the Shanghai Municipal Police.

ch06.anchor: construction detail for chemical and explosive munitions
ch06.note: Translator's note. The original Section 4 closes with the internal make-up of the gas-gun cartridge and then a subsection on 炸彈 (explosive charges). That material is step-by-step construction detail for chemical and explosive munitions, and it has been withheld from this edition as dangerous how-to content. Only its place in the argument is marked, so that the surrounding structure and cross-references stay intact.

ch06.anchor: the art of destruction
ch06.note: Translator's note. Only the non-technical doctrine of Section 5 is given in this edition: its rationale, its political forms, the four modes it names, and the organization of a sabotage cell. The section's technical core — the construction, charging and emplacement of explosive and chemical devices — is withheld as dangerous how-to content. Unlike the rest of the book, these passages were rendered from OCR under a deliberate limit of not closely reading the construction pages, so the readings are more provisional than elsewhere.

ch06.anchor: A hundred sicknesses enter by the mouth
ch06.note: A common Chinese proverb, 病從口入，禍從口出 (“sickness enters by the mouth, calamity issues from the mouth”), traditionally traced to the Jin-dynasty writer Fu Xuan (傅玄). It pairs a warning about diet with one about careless speech; the author invokes only the second half.

ch06.anchor: the golden man with his mouth thrice sealed
ch06.note: An allusion to 金人三緘其口. In 說苑·敬慎 and 孔子家語·觀周, Confucius, visiting the ancestral temple of Zhou, finds a bronze statue (“golden man”) whose mouth is sealed three times over, its back inscribed: “This was a man of old careful in speech. Take warning! Say little, for many words bring many defeats.” It became the byword for guarded speech.

ch06.anchor: the man who cannot read a face goes hungry
ch06.note: A colloquial saying — roughly “the illiterate can still eat, but the man who cannot read a situation goes hungry.” 識相 (shixiang), “to read a face / take the hint,” is a Wu-dialect (Shanghai) expression; the proverb prizes social tact over book-learning.

ch06.anchor: know many men and be known by few
ch06.note: The maxim 要知人者多，被人知者少 (“know many, be known by few”) is a piece of tradecraft doctrine: the agent's asymmetry of knowledge is his protection. It restates in aphorism the recurring rule of the manual that one gathers all one can about others while yielding nothing of oneself.

ch06.anchor: To interrogate a political prisoner by torture and beating can settle nothing
ch06.note: The passage is notable in that the author — formerly the Communist Party's own security and assassination chief before his 1931 defection — expressly rejects torture (非刑拷打) in favour of interrogation by conversation and rapport-building. 政治犯 (“political prisoner”) is the period term for those detained for their party affiliation or activity.

ch06.anchor: bringing him to sanction
ch06.note: “Sanction” renders 制裁 (zhicai), the manual's standing euphemism for killing — the liquidation of a target. The book sets it against 破壞 (sabotage) as the direct way of eliminating an enemy, sabotage being the indirect.

ch06.anchor: looking on death as a homecoming
ch06.note: 視死如歸, a classical idiom (found in the Guanzi and the Han Feizi, and famous from the Records of the Three Kingdoms) for one who faces death without fear, “as if going home.” Here it is listed, coldly, as a hiring qualification for a saboteur — alongside “without kin and without ties.”

ch06.anchor: what common talk calls
ch06.note: 切口 (qiēkǒu) is the argot of a trade or a secret society — a private vocabulary that lets insiders speak in the open without outsiders following. The word recurs throughout this section.

ch06.anchor: the Green and Red Gangs
ch06.note: The Green Gang (青幫) and Red Gang (紅幫) were the great sworn brotherhoods of Republican-era China, rooted in the Yangtze grain-boatmen's guilds and, by the 1920s–30s, dominant in Shanghai's underworld (Du Yuesheng's Green Gang is the best known). Each kept an elaborate secret argot, which is Gu's point here. Corroborated by the standard scholarship on Chinese secret societies.

ch06.anchor: he wants the Red Dragon
ch06.note: The illustration is drawn from mahjong played in collusion. The Red, White, and Green Dragons (中／紅中, 白板, 發財) are the three honor "dragon" tiles; the "one of Bamboo," "one of Circles," and "one of Characters" (一條, 一筒, 一萬) are the 1 of each of the three suits. Confederates signal which tile they need by a prearranged gesture.

ch06.anchor: wei, chen, yue, shan, geng
ch06.note: The wheel's code-names are the traditional cyclical signs: the ten Heavenly Stems (甲乙丙丁戊己庚辛壬癸) and twelve Earthly Branches (子丑寅卯辰巳午未申酉戌亥), together with 天地日月山水金木 (Heaven, Earth, Sun, Moon, Mountain, Water, Metal, Wood). Of the code words here, wei (未), chen (辰), shen (申), hai (亥), and zi (子) are Earthly Branches; jia (甲) and geng (庚) are Heavenly Stems; shan (山) and mu (木) and yue (月) come from the elemental set.

ch06.anchor: Look at the means a man employs
ch06.note: Analects II.10 (為政篇): 視其所以，觀其所由，察其所安 — "Look at the means a man employs, observe the springs of his conduct, examine what gives him rest." Gu borrows Confucius to dignify a chapter of character-judging, and turns the three clauses into the headings of his points 2 and 3.

ch06.anchor: holding a post and eating the bread of idleness
ch06.note: 尸位素餐 — literally "to fill the seat like a corpse and eat the bread for nothing," i.e. to draw the pay of an office while doing none of its work. A classical idiom (from the Book of Documents and the Book of Han).

ch06.anchor: People gather by their kind
ch06.note: 人以類聚，物以羣分 — "people gather by their kind, things divide by their sort," a proverb whose source is the Xici commentary to the Book of Changes (物以類聚，人以群分).

ch06.anchor: not to set up as fortune-tellers
ch06.note: 形相術 (also 相術) is traditional Chinese physiognomy, the reading of character and fortune from face and body. Gu recasts it as a practical skill for judging agents rather than as divination; but the content that follows — the humoral "constitutions," the feature-by-feature verdicts — is the folk physiognomy of the period, not science. It is translated here as the author's belief, not endorsed.

ch06.anchor: the innate constitution of mankind falls into four different types
ch06.note: The four "constitutions" — 神經質 (nervous), 膽汁質 (bilious), 多血質 (sanguine), and 粘膜質 (lymphatic/mucous) — are a Chinese rendering of the old European doctrine of the four temperaments (nervous, choleric, sanguine, phlegmatic), themselves descended from classical humoral medicine. Gu grounds them in heredity and a prenatal "chemical stimulus."

ch06.anchor: pretty-boy
ch06.note: 小白臉 (xiǎo báiliǎn), "little white face" — a fair, soft-featured young man, with an undertone of the kept lover or gigolo.

ch06.anchor: cheeks that show from behind the head
ch06.note: 腦後見腮, "cheeks visible from behind the head" — a fixed physiognomic sign, read traditionally as the mark of a treacherous and ungrateful nature (compare 反骨, the "bone of rebellion").

ch06.anchor: hides a knife within his smile
ch06.note: 笑裏藏刀, "a knife hidden in the smile" — a classical idiom (and one of the Thirty-Six Stratagems) for concealed malice behind a friendly face.

ch06.anchor: Concerning the Five Features and their placing
ch06.note: 五官, the "Five Features" of Chinese physiognomy — conventionally the ears, eyebrows, eyes, nose, and mouth; the term also stands for the face as a whole.

ch06.anchor: just come green into the world
ch06.note: 初出茅廬, "just out of the thatched hut" — a novice, still untried; from the tale of Zhuge Liang, who left his thatched cottage to serve Liu Bei and won his first campaign at once.

ch06.anchor: the threadbare pedant
ch06.note: 窮措大 — an old, faintly contemptuous term for an impoverished scholar: the shabby-genteel man of letters with more learning than money.

ch06.anchor: the planchette (扶乩)
ch06.note: Four folk-occult practices, all of which Gu explains as unwitting hypnotism: 扶乩 (fújī), planchette or spirit-writing, a suspended stylus tracing characters said to be dictated by a god; 圓光 (yuánguāng), scrying a spirit-image in a mirror or on paper; 關亡 (guānwáng), a medium's summoning of a dead soul; and 請麻姑, the calling-down of the Taoist immortal Ma Gu.

ch06.anchor: an Austrian psychiatrist
ch06.note: The book's history is loose. The figure it has in mind is almost certainly Franz Anton Mesmer (1734–1815), the Austrian physician whose "animal magnetism" (mesmerism) is the ancestor of hypnotic practice — hence the "electromagnetic induction" invoked below. But Mesmer was no psychiatrist, and the word "hypnotism" was coined later by the Scottish surgeon James Braid, who rejected Mesmer's magnetic fluid. The attribution is uncorroborated as stated.

ch06.anchor: an old monk sunk in meditative trance
ch06.note: 入定 (rùdìng), "entering dìng" — the meditative absorption (Sanskrit samādhi) of Buddhist practice, in which the mind is stilled to a single point. Gu uses it as the familiar image of total concentration.

ch06.anchor: thousand-li eye
ch06.note: Three claimed powers: 千里眼 (the "thousand-li eye," clairvoyant sight at a distance — also the name of a temple guardian deity), 透視 (seeing through solid objects), and 意想傳通術 (thought-transmission, i.e. telepathy). Gu presents them as genuine effects of hypnotism; there is no scientific basis for any of them.

ch06.anchor: at least f5 or better
ch06.note: f5 is the lens aperture (f-number); the smaller the number, the wider the opening and the more light admitted, which is what allows the fast exposures Gu wants for candid work in poor light. Modern notation writes it f/5.

ch06.anchor: the pistol type, the matchbox type
ch06.note: Concealed or "detective" cameras built into everyday objects — watches, matchboxes, cigarette packets, walking-sticks, and even pistols — were a real and much-advertised class of apparatus from the 1880s on (the Stirn waistcoat camera and the various book- and cane-cameras are documented examples). Corroborated.

ch06.anchor: the reflection of ultraviolet is very strong
ch06.note: The physics is roughly right for the orthochromatic dry-plates of the day, which were sensitive to blue and ultraviolet but nearly blind to red: green foliage and warm evening light, poor in the blue and UV the plate needed, under-exposed, while a bright overcast sky or a white wall, rich in scattered UV, over-exposed. Judging this by eye, as Gu says, was a genuine skill.

ch07.note: Dǎ chéng yī piàn (打成一片), literally “to beat or knead into a single piece” — to merge with a milieu until one is indistinguishable from it. It is the governing verb of this section and is rendered “become one with society” throughout; the section title 社會化 (“blending into society”) is the noun of the same idea.

Two idioms of futility set side by side: chīrén shuō mèng (癡人說夢), “a fool recounting his dreams,” and bìng zhōng yìyǔ (病中囈語), “raving in a fever.” Both mean talk wholly cut loose from what is possible.

ch07.anchor: mere parasites and vermin upon society
ch07.note: The source is 附庸和蟊賊: fùyōng, a dependent appendage with no standing of its own, and máozéi, properly the insects that devour young crops — hence those who feed on and ruin the common good.

ch07.anchor: spent on the blade's edge, not on its back
ch07.note: A vivid saying, 錢要用在刀口上，不要用在刀背上: spend money where it does the cutting (the edge), not where it is wasted (the blunt back of the blade).

ch07.anchor: fond of being fitted with a tall hat
ch07.note: Dài gāomàozi (戴高帽子), “to put a tall hat on someone” — to flatter.

ch07.anchor: a hand to fill out the scene
ch07.note: The source is bāng chǎng (幫場), from the theater: to swell an audience or back up a performer, hence to lend a friend visible support so that he keeps face.

ch07.anchor: the will is there but not the strength
ch07.note: The idiom xīn yǒu yú ér lì bù zú (心有餘而力不足): the willingness is there but not the capacity.

ch07.anchor: where three walk together, one is sure to be my teacher
ch07.note: From the Analects (VII.22), Confucius: 三人行必有我師, “when three walk together, one of them is sure to be my teacher” — there is something to be learned from anyone.

ch07.anchor: a warning from the cart ahead
ch07.note: Qián chē zhī jiàn (前車之鑒): the cart overturned ahead is a warning to the one behind; a cautionary precedent.

The Hai-Lu-Feng uprising (海陸豐, the counties of Haifeng and Lufeng in eastern Guangdong), led by Peng Pai: the short-lived Hailufeng Soviet, proclaimed in November 1927, was crushed by early 1928. The book’s placing of the CCP’s regrouping in Shanghai just after this failure is corroborated by the standard accounts.

ch07.anchor: the winter of 1927, when the Nationalists and the Communists parted ways
ch07.note: 國共分家, the collapse of the First United Front in 1927 — Chiang Kai-shek’s purge of the Communists at Shanghai in April and the Wuhan government’s break with them in July — which drove the CCP underground and set the stage for the secret-service work described here.

ch07.anchor: At first only one section was established
ch07.note: This is the founding of the CCP’s Central Special Branch (中央特科, the “Teke”), the Party’s first professional intelligence and security service. Scholarship dates its establishment to November 1927, designed by Zhou Enlai with Xiang Zhongfa and the author himself, Gu Shunzhang; the book, written by Gu, dates the formal footing to January 1928. Its four sections match the record: the First (General Affairs), Second (Intelligence), Third (Action — the assassination squad known as the 紅隊 or “Red Squad,” which the book calls “Protection”), and Fourth (clandestine radio Communications). Corroborated (Wikipedia, “Central Special Branch”).

ch07.anchor: the horse that harms the herd
ch07.note: Hài qún zhī mǎ (害羣之馬), “the horse that brings harm to the herd” — the black sheep who endangers the group; here the man who surrenders to the authorities or turns informer.

ch07.anchor: for every day they put out an intelligence sheet
ch07.note: The source names a daily intelligence bulletin, 「敏捷飛」, romanized here Minjie Fei and literally “the Swift Flyer.” The three characters are scan-verified, but the title is an internal coinage not otherwise attested, and the rendering is provisional.

ch07.anchor: A most unfortunate incident befell them
ch07.note: The “most unfortunate incident” of the twentieth year of the Republic (1931) is the author’s own arrest at Wuhan in April 1931 and his defection to the Nationalists, which rolled up the CCP’s Shanghai underground almost overnight. Gu here narrates his own betrayal obliquely, in the third person; see the note at Chapter 5 on the same disaster. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: drive deep into the Nationalists' secret-service organization
ch07.note: The CCP did penetrate the Nationalists’ intelligence apparatus at its highest level: Qian Zhuangfei, Li Kenong, and Hu Di worked inside the investigation section of the Nationalist Central Organization Department (the forerunner of the “CC Clique” service, later the Zhongtong). It was Qian’s warning, sent after Gu’s own defection, that let the CCP leadership in Shanghai escape arrest. Corroborated.
A front business, 信誼代辦所, a general commission-agency that would transact any errand on a client’s behalf; Xinyi (“good faith”) is taken here as its name. The rendering is provisional.

流氓運動, literally “hoodlum activity” — organizing the lumpen underworld of toughs, gangsters and drifters. The never-formed Fifth Section points ahead to this chapter’s fourth section, 下層社會的研究 (“the study of society’s lower strata”), and to the manual’s recurring interest in bending the underworld to secret-service ends.

The Cheka (Russian ВЧК, the All-Russian Extraordinary Commission; 非常委員會), founded in December 1917 under Dzerzhinsky. It was abolished in February 1922 and its work passed to the GPU (格伯武, ГПУ, the State Political Directorate), which in November 1923 was reorganized as the OGPU; the book treats GPU and OGPU as one and the same, and renders both “the GPU” (see the glossary and the note at Chapter 1). The “Red Defense Corps” the book places “under the Tsar” is loose — the Red Guards proper date to 1917. Corroborated (Wikipedia; the Seventeen Moments in Soviet History archive).

The words are attributed to Stalin. He did publicly extol the GPU and its successor the OGPU in just these terms — as the drawn sword of the proletarian dictatorship and the terror of the counter-revolution. The exact wording quoted here has not been traced to a specific published text, but the substance is faithful to Stalin’s stated view.

ch07.anchor: Trotsky's Opposition and the cadre faction
ch07.note: The intra-Bolshevik struggle of the 1920s between Trotsky’s Left Opposition and the Party apparatus — the 幹部派 or “cadre faction,” meaning Stalin’s machine — which ended in Trotsky’s expulsion from the Party in 1927 and his exile from the USSR in 1929. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: the White Russians and other reactionary combinations
ch07.note: The “Whites” (白俄, White Russians), the anti-Bolshevik armies of the Russian Civil War of 1918–22, backed by the “intervention of the Powers” (列強干涉, the Allied intervention) that the next clause names. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: he must besides be one of the members of the Party's Central Politburo
ch07.note: Overstated. The chief of the OGPU in these years, Vyacheslav Menzhinsky (chairman 1926–34), sat on the Party’s Central Committee but was not a member of the Politburo. The requirement the book states is not documented.

ch07.anchor: the branch directorates of the six republics
ch07.note: By 1933 the USSR comprised seven union republics — the RSFSR plus six others — so the book’s scheme of a Moscow head directorate over “the other six republics’” branches matches the count of the day. (The number of union republics rose to eleven only under the 1936 constitution.) Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: a fully-armed force of one hundred thousand men
ch07.note: The GPU and OGPU kept their own internal-security and border troops, drawn partly from the Red Army; a strength on the order of a hundred thousand is plausible for the early 1930s. Corroborated in kind.

The book’s claim — that in the Cheka era the body could arrest anyone from Central Committee members downward save Lenin — is the author’s characterization, not a documented rule; but it conveys the Cheka’s recognized extra-legal reach. Uncorroborated as a formal rule.

ch07.anchor: the nine streams and three teachings
ch07.note: Jiuliu sanjiao (九流三教), literally “the nine streams and three teachings” — a fixed phrase that once named the classical schools of thought and here stands loosely for the whole run of itinerant folk trades: fortune-tellers, quacks, gamblers, brothel-keepers, thieves and the like. The author uses it for all who, in his words, scrape a living by their wits on the road (混江湖).

青龍棍, also called the 家法棍 (“staves of family law”). In Green Gang legend these emperor-granted staves are the badge of the order’s founding charge to guard the imperial grain convoys, and they figure in its initiation lore.

羅祖, “Patriarch Luo.” Green Gang tradition traces the order to a religious teacher surnamed Luo, identified with Luo Qing (羅清, c. 1443–1527), the mid-Ming founder of the Wuwei or Luo sect (羅教), whose scriptures were carried among the Grand Canal boatmen. The book’s foundation story — the Jiajing-17 (1538) date, the miracle of red rain and red flowers, the three sworn patriarchs — is gang legend, not documented history: Luo Qing died in 1527, and the boatmen’s brotherhood from which the Green Gang actually grew is dated by scholarship to the Yongzheng reign (1726). Corroborated as the gang’s own traditional account; the dating is not historical.

翁、錢、潘 — the “three patriarchs” (三祖) of Green Gang tradition: Weng Yan (翁巖), Qian Jian (錢堅) and Pan Qing (潘清), said to have organized the grain-transport boatmen under an imperial commission and to have founded, in the Yongzheng reign, the seventy-two-and-a-half wharves and the gangs of the canal grain fleet. Corroborated as the gang’s traditional account.

洪楊, shorthand for Hong Xiuquan (洪秀全) and Yang Xiuqing (楊秀清), the paramount leaders of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom (1851–1864); “洪楊” is a common Republican-era name for the Taiping Rebellion. That the Red Gang split from the Green Gang about the time of the Taiping’s fall is gang tradition, not established fact.

ch07.anchor: destroy the Qing and restore the Ming
ch07.note: 滅清復明, a variant of the anti-Manchu slogan 反清復明 (“oppose the Qing, restore the Ming”) common to the Qing-era secret societies; its attachment to the Green Gang belongs to that shared founding rhetoric.

Huang Jinrong (黃金榮), Du Yuesheng (杜月笙, introduced in Chapter 6) and Zhang Xiaolin (張嘯林) were the “three tycoons” (三大亨) who ran the Green Gang of the French Concession. The “great opium company” is the Sanxin Company (三鑫公司, founded 1918), the opium-transport “insurance” monopoly they held with the Concession police behind them; at its height its profits were reckoned at a third of the government’s revenue. All corroborated. A period saying summed the three: Huang greedy for money, Zhang good with his fists, Du a maker of men.

Huang Chujiu (黃楚九, 1872–1931), the entrepreneur behind Shanghai’s patent-medicine trade and the Great World (大世界) amusement hall. The book’s remark that he was not a gang member is apt — he in fact lost the Great World to Huang Jinrong. Corroborated.
Green Gang cant for an outsider or mark: 洋盤 (“foreign platter”), 空子 (“empty one”) and 大菜盤 (“big [Western-]dinner dish”) — all names for the man who is not in the gang and so may be gulled.

The gang’s argot (切口) for the police is given largely by sound: 彫林碼子 for a uniformed constable, 三光碼子 for a plainclothes detective (碼子, “a figure,” a cant suffix). These romanizations are provisional; the terms are local Shanghai gang slang, not otherwise attested.

The Green Gang’s generation-name poem (輩分/字派), by which a member’s seniority is fixed. The widely-cited standard first twenty-four characters read 清淨道德、文成佛法、能仁智慧、本來自信、元明興理、大通悟學; the book has 仁倫 for 能仁 and 與禮 for 興理, minor variants. The last characters 大、通、悟、學 are the generations named in item h, and place Du Yuesheng in the “Tong” (通) generation.

海底 (“sea-bottom”), the Green Gang’s secret handbook of lineage and rules, also called the 通草, the 金不換 (“not to be exchanged for gold”) or the 同錄 — comparable to the lodge-books of the Hongmen societies.
The name (李則高) is scan-verified but not otherwise attested; the romanization is provisional.

花會, the “flower-club” lottery, a hugely popular illegal numbers game in Republican Shanghai. The banker seals away one of thirty-six “gates” (thirty-seven in the Chaozhou version), each named for a mythological figure — the first, Wu Zhankui, being the White-Fish Spirit — and players bet on which he has chosen; a hit pays about thirty for one. Corroborated as a notorious racket of the period.
The reputed head of the Shanghai flower-club racket is given as 癩頭筋鮑方, “Scabby-head Tendon Bao Fang” (a nickname plus a name). Scan-verified but not otherwise attested; rendered provisionally.

The Shanghai courtesan-house hierarchy. The changsan (長三) was the first class — the name traditionally explained by a flat fee of three yuan for a call and three for a banquet; the yao’er (么二, “one-two”) the second. This graded demimonde is well documented (see Christian Henriot, Prostitution and Sexuality in Shanghai).
鹹肉莊, literally “salted-meat house” — a low brothel, also called a 韓莊 (“Han house”) by a play on the near-homophone. The literal image is the point of the slang.

Fourth Avenue (四馬路, today’s Fuzhou Road) was Shanghai’s notorious street of brothels and cheap pleasures. The 野雞 (“wild chickens,” i.e. pheasants) are the unlicensed streetwalkers who tout there and along the lanes named.

鹹水妹, “salt-water girls” — Cantonese prostitutes of the treaty ports who served foreign sailors, the term usually taken from their sea-going (“salt-water”) clientele. A recognized category of the period.

The source has 洋涇浜英語, “Yangjingbang English.” The Yangjingbang (洋涇浜) was the creek dividing the foreign settlements, and its name became the Shanghai word for the pidgin spoken between Chinese and foreigners. Corroborated.

ch07.anchor: The swindler gangs have both men and women
ch07.note: 拆白黨, professional swindler-and-badger gangs that worked the seduction con for money. The “insurance gang” (保險黨) described next — luring a man, insuring his life, then doing away with him for the payout — is the more lurid variant.

仙人跳, “the immortal’s leap” — the classic badger game: a woman lures a man into a compromising position, whereupon confederates posing as her outraged menfolk burst in and extort him. The name is proverbial.

肉票, literally “flesh ticket” — underworld term for a kidnap hostage (票, “ticket,” being the ransom object). The “ticket” vocabulary — 綁票, “to bind a ticket,” i.e. to kidnap — runs through this passage.

嵊縣 (now Shengzhou), in eastern Zhejiang, carried a Republican-era reputation as a nursery of professional kidnap gangs working Shanghai; 架人 and 接財神 (“welcoming the god of wealth”) are their cant for the trade. The specific attribution is a period commonplace and is not independently corroborated here.

The thieves’ stupefying agents: 悶香 (“swoon-incense,” a smoke or powder of folklore) and 以特 (also written 以脫), a transliteration of “ether,” which the book says could be had over a pharmacy counter. Reading 以特 as “ether” is the natural sense, but it is a transliteration, not an attested name.
剝豬玀, literally “skinning the pigs” — cant for footpads who waylay passersby and strip them of their clothes (worth most in winter). The older name given is 揹娘舅, “carrying the maternal uncle.”
辰州 (Chenzhou, in western Hunan) was famed for its Daoist talismanic magic — the “Chenzhou talismans” (辰州符) — from which the scrying trick (圓光, glossed earlier) is here said to derive.

ch07.anchor: one hitting the mark upon another
ch07.note: The trick turns on graphs that cannot survive translation. 串 (“string”) is read as two 中 (“to hit the mark; to pass”) stacked one upon another — hence “pass upon pass.” But set a 心 (“heart”) beneath 串 and it becomes 患 (“calamity”) — hence the second man’s certain failure. The whole was cold reading; the graph, as the author says, had nothing to do with it.
The source reads 數十八 (“some ten-and-eight”), which does not parse as a clean figure and is almost certainly a misprint for 數十 (“some tens”); rendered here as “some tens.”

ch08.note: The chapter's title word is xiūyǎng (修養), “cultivation” — the Confucian vocabulary of moral self-improvement (cf. xiūshēn 修身, “cultivating the person,” in the Great Learning). Gu takes this classical language of the gentleman's inner discipline and turns it to the training of a secret agent's character. The redeployment is deliberate and runs through the chapter; “cultivation” is kept for 修養 throughout.

Kuàdǎng fènzǐ (跨黨份子), literally “straddling-the-parties elements” — those holding membership in two parties at once. During the First United Front (1923–1927) Communists joined the Nationalist Party as individuals while keeping their CCP membership; after Chiang Kai-shek's purge of April 1927 the term hardened into the standard Nationalist label for Communists concealed within Nationalist ranks. The point is pointed: Gu Shunzhang had himself been the Chinese Communist Party's chief of security and intelligence until his defection to the Nationalists in April 1931, and this manual is the defector's counsel to his new masters on how to root out exactly such hidden men. The historical frame is well corroborated in the scholarship on the United Front and on Gu's defection (e.g. Frederic Wakeman, Policing Shanghai, 1927–1937).

Zuì shēng mèng sǐ (醉生夢死), “drunk in life, dreaming in death” — to fritter one's days away in a fuddled stupor, oblivious of any higher purpose. A Song-dynasty coinage (attributed to Cheng Yi), long since a fixed idiom.

ch08.anchor: a tiger's head only to trail away like a snake's tail
ch08.note: Hǔ tóu shé wěi (虎頭蛇尾), “tiger's head, snake's tail” — to begin with a grand flourish and dwindle to nothing. Kept literal here for its vividness.

Jiǔ sè cái qì (酒色財氣), “wine, lust, wealth, wrath” — the traditional Chinese tetrad of the four besetting vices, proverbially the “four walls” (酒色財氣四堵牆) that hem a man in. It is a stock set of the popular moralists; Gu keeps the fourfold frame and gives each vice its tradecraft gloss (drink loosens secrets, sex is a lever and a trap, money buys men, temper unseats judgment).

ch08.anchor: offering an umbrella after the rain
ch08.note: Yǔ hòu sòng sǎn (雨後送傘), “to send an umbrella after the rain” — help or action that comes too late to be of any use. The image is kept literal.

ch08.anchor: If you do not enter the tiger's den, how shall you take the tiger's cub?
ch08.note: Bù rù hǔ xué, yān dé hǔ zǐ (不入虎穴，焉得虎子) — nothing ventured, nothing gained. The words are those of the Han envoy-general Ban Chao, rallying his small party to a night attack during his mission to the Western Regions in 73 CE, as recorded in the Book of the Later Han (後漢書, “Biography of Ban Chao”). A classical locus, correctly invoked.

ch08.anchor: For him who has the will, the thing is in the end accomplished
ch08.note: Yǒu zhì zhě, shì jìng chéng (有志者，事竟成), “where there is a will, the deed is at last done.” The phrase is the Emperor Guangwu's praise of his general Geng Yan, in the Book of the Later Han (後漢書, “Biography of Geng Yan”). Correctly attributed to proverb; the book quotes it as a stock maxim.

ch08.anchor: A little impatience overturns a great plan
ch08.note: Xiǎo bù rěn, zé luàn dà móu (小不忍，則亂大謀), from the Analects (論語, “Wei Ling Gong,” 15.27): “Clever words confound virtue; a want of forbearance in small things confounds great designs.” It is the book's closing exhortation — and here the surviving text of it breaks off. The final leaf of the book (printed folio 237, which would have completed this sentence and closed the chapter) is missing from the National Central Library scan: the scanner double-fed folio 235 where folio 237 should be, and the leaf that follows is blank. The publisher's errata table corrects nothing past folio 236, so at most a sentence or two is lost. No bridging text has been supplied; the translation stops exactly where the scan does.
A cross-reference to Chapter 5 of this book (秘密, “Secrecy”), where the handling of secrets is treated at length. The back-reference confirms the book's own chapter order.
Shí fēn zhī shí (十分之十), “ten parts out of ten” — a colloquial intensive, i.e. wholly, a hundred per cent. Kept literal to preserve the reckoning idiom.
